title: Is Anyone Interested In Caligula- Ultimate Cut?

commenti.body: [removed]

Yes and no. History is one of my favourite genres, and I miss the grandeur and largesse and overall earnestness of the better historical epics of yore.

At the same time, I actually feel like a lot of those films - especially those set in Graeco-Roman times - could get quite cheesy, and I feel like the novelty of Caligula over the run-of-the-mill epics probably *was* the pornographic aspect of it.

I'll probably check it out when it's cheap and easy to get ahold of, since I've always seen Caligula as an interesting cinematic oddity, but my expectations aren't terribly high.

The truth is:  (1) Gore Vidal has been dead for the past eleven years.  His vision for the film died with him.  (2) The movie was directed by a softcore pornographer, so there probably isn't high art hidden anywhere in his footage.  (3) The restoration isn't being handled by a filmmaker with a clear artistic vision.  It's just some guy.

The version that was recently screened and introduced by Helen Mirren at a festival? Yeah, I'm interested. If I'm remembering right it does things like restore the "good" acting takes that were invariably left unused in place of the more over the top ones, and clears up some of the mess. From reading reactions it still has much the effect of older cuts though, that is to say a mixture of striking opulence, campy outrage and genuine nastiness that is both indictment and kind of into it. I don't think there's any chance of making it a genuinely "good" film that doesn't involve a time machine (I mean, given that Brass' best is probably Salon Kitty), and I like the current circulating longest print just fine, it's a trash landmark, but given the calibre of the actors it seems like a worthwhile experiment at least to bring them out better.

Not in a theatre, but as a home watch with friends and beers. It's apex so-bad-it's-great hilarity.

As for how it even got made, the 70s were bananas and, like the last days of Rome, packed with terrible decisions. The guilt-free hedonism enjoyed by a privileged few in the 60s lost its last vestiges of morality when it went mainstream in the decade of debauchery and everyone started doing whatever they wanted. Society became so untethered it took AIDS, crack and an unprecedented violent crime explosion to get everyone to calm down, start doing aerobics and get very obsessed with making it,  money and material goods.

The late 90s got pretty wild in the run up to the millennium too. But the 70s were something else. New York 1977: the Hottest Year in Hell is a great snapshot of a city tipping over into complete chaos.At one point, just like Rome, the Bronx actually burns.

Looking at comments here and elsewhere about the film makes me realize I'm in a miniscule (delusional?) minority that believes the 156 minute cut is a genuinely fantastic film. That being said, I am interested and excited to check out this entirely different cut. I'm hoping we get a release on blu-ray with as many cuts as they can give us, as it's a fascinating battle of differing visions.

Just curious what leads you to believe the filmmaker doesn't have a clear artistic vision. Wasn't the goal to try to achieve what Vidal seemed to want? Though not necessarily personal or original, that seems like a clear artistic vision, maybe even moreso than in the various cuts we've seen so far.

Thomas Negovan is an inexperienced filmmaker. Even if he intended to restore Gore's cut, it's unlikely he would have the skill to do so.

The narrative surrounding the 1980 cut isn't about Gore being denied final cut. Gore's script was changed before it was ever shot. You can't restore how version because it was never filmed. The injustice of the old cut is that it was some without the director's involvement. There were plans to restore the director's cut before Penthouse decided to ditch that and deprive Tinto Brass of a director's cut a second time. You have to be kind of mercenary to do something like that.

Negovan's cut is basically a fan edit financed by Penthouse to capitalize on interest in a restoration - but this isn't a real restoration. It's another Penthouse cut that has nothing to do with Brass or Gore. It's Negovan, who is a complete rando.
Give us the Tinto Brass cut

Fair enough. I don't hold him being inexperienced as a strike against him, especially since the actual directorial duties were largely done, and with Merhige watching over the edit (he is still involved, right?) I feel like there's some genuine creative talent and experience ultimately involved.

I always chuckle at the thought what Sir John Gielgud said with earnest pride: I think I just stared in my first pornographic film.  
The source for this quote, if anyone is interested, is an memory of british film critic Mark Kermode.
It would be interesting. I have seen the film and there is a more classic swords and sandals film lurking in there. Certainly adult, but then the story of Caligula is hardly for the kids.

I don’t think it’s entirely fair to say that Brass was deprived a director’s cut. Brass was never planned to be directly involved with the previous restoration attempt, they were just planning on emulating his directing style with his good graces. Negovan reached out to Brass to be involved with this cut but understandably a 90 yr old man has better things to do with his time than revisit an old wound like Caligula

And it’s also important to keep in mind that there’s a team of people involved in this cut, so just because Negovan doesn’t have much film experience himself doesn’t mean everyone involved is inexperienced. 

It’s easy to be pessimistic with how Penthouse has handled Caligula in the past, but it seems to me from the materials they’ve released that real care has been put into marrying everyone’s visions for this cut.

I wouldn’t say the Ultimate Cut aims to follow Vidal’s script (and that’s probably for the best). Like others have pointed out, the script changed a lot from Vidal’s original before they started filming, so there’s no way to recreate it from what they have. Rather, the Ultimate Cut follows the intuition of the actors (McDowell especially, who was even credited as one of the writers in the original for the amount of work he put in to clean up the script) and the performances they gave. Personally I think that’s the best way to “restore” Caligula to what it should have been, without the huge clash of egos between Vidal, Brass, and Guccioni.
And besides, McDowell already carried the movie with his amazing performance, who wouldn’t want to see a more faithful depiction of the movie he actually *thought* he was making?
I’m fairly certain he loved when he saw it, McDowell said Gielgud saw it several times. He like me fr.

Fuck. Yes. 
I personally love the original cut as flawed as it is. The film is a masterpiece and I think this new cut will help a larger audience understand it better. Also Bob Guccione added the 10 or so extra minutes of unnecessary porn much later in the editing process with Penthouse Pets. By that time all of the actors had long since agreed and filmed all their parts.
